summary:
Alabama prohibits transgender people from using public bathrooms and facilities in line with their gender identity under state bans enacted in 2022 and 2024, as tabulated by the Movement Advancement Project's equality map. A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places Alabama in its worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions, citing a bathroom ban carried by the state's 'Don't Say Gay' legislation that extends to college campuses.

The school-level facility rule is statutory. House Bill 261's predecessor, HB322, signed 8 April 2022 as Act No. 2022-290, requires public school students to use bathrooms consistent with the gender on their birth certificate, a requirement codified by the Alabama Board of Education in September 2022. A March 2024 bill would extend the restriction to university bathrooms not aligned with sex assigned at birth. Senate Bill 79, signed in February 2025, declares gender an immutable male-female binary determined by biological sex assigned at birth and permits separate single-sex spaces wherever biology, privacy, safety or fairness are invoked.

Gender-affirming care for minors is a felony offence. Under the Vulnerable Child Compassion and Protection Act (SB 184), signed 8 April 2022 and enforceable from 8 May 2022, a medical provider who gives puberty blockers, hormones or surgery to anyone under 19 commits a Class C felony punishable by 10 years in prison. The Eleventh Circuit allowed enforcement from 21 August 2023, and the ban has remained in force since plaintiffs withdrew their challenge on 1 May 2025.

Alabama's document rules require surgical intervention. The state permits amendment of a birth certificate or driver's licence to the current sex only on documentation of sex "changed by surgical procedure" together with a name change. A January 2021 federal ruling in Corbitt v. Taylor invalidated the surgery requirement, but the Eleventh Circuit reversed it; on 20 September 2024 the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals held that refusing to issue accurate licences does not violate the federal constitution, rehearing was denied on 13 November 2024 and judgment entered 10 December 2024. The ACLU states that most transgender people therefore cannot obtain an accurate licence and must carry daily identification showing the wrong gender, which exposes them to a high risk of harassment and violence during ID checks.

Sporting participation is restricted at both school and college level. House Bill 391, enacted in April 2021 after passing the House 74-19 with two abstentions and signed by Governor Kay Ivey, requires all K-12 athletes to compete in teams based on the gender listed on their birth certificate. Since 1 July 2021 public schools must assign single-sex teams by "biological sex," and House Bill 261, signed 30 May 2023, prohibits college and university competition on a team differing from sex assigned at birth even after gender-affirming hormone therapy, except in co-ed sports.

The Needle's national analysis of July 2026, using TGEU and Williams Institute data, records Alabama's rate of killings of trans women at 3.8 per 100,000 per year. That figure is a population-adjusted rate rather than a raw count, and the analysis describes it as an undercount floor computed on a 428-victim base covering 2008-2025. The same analysis grades Alabama in the worst-law group.

A trans visitor has no statewide recourse against discrimination. Alabama has no law prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations or student harassment and bullying, and imposes no ban on insurance exclusions for transgender healthcare and provides no transgender-inclusive health benefits to state employees. The practical effect is denial of care, exclusion from gendered facilities and no public-accommodations remedy. Only Birmingham, since September 2017, and Montevallo, since April 2018, prohibit all such discrimination, while Huntsville, Tuscaloosa and Montgomery provide public-employment protections.

The state's hate-crime law, in force since 1994, covers race, colour, religion, national origin, ethnicity and physical or mental disability only, and does not apply to offences motivated by gender identity. Federal coverage exists under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act signed in October 2009, and in Eleventh Circuit jurisdiction gender identity has been applied to sex under Title VII since 2011.

All Alabama counties have recorded marriage certificates for all couples, including couples Alabama would class as same-sex, since 29 August 2019, following a May 2019 legislative requirement that ended eight counties' refusal to record licences. Alabama permits adoption by same-sex couples, though the Supreme Court of Alabama held in 2002 that homosexual conduct created a strong presumption of parental unfitness, and the Child Placing Agency Inclusion Act of May 2017, signed by Governor Kay Ivey, protects faith-based agencies that refuse placements on religious grounds.
tangentialFactors:
Alabama is grouped with the most restrictive states by two separate 2026 assessments: a July 2026 anti-trans legal risk map, which classes it among legislatively-erasing jurisdictions, and The Needle's July 2026 analysis, which grades it in the worst-law group. Both gradings turn on the state's own statutes rather than on national measures.

2025 statewide polling places Alabama among the lowest-support states for transgender-inclusive nondiscrimination and access policies, which bears on the likelihood of local discretion, complaint handling or informal accommodation in practice.

The state's legacy statutes on sexual orientation have been cleared at intervals: the requirement that sex education describe homosexuality as an unacceptable lifestyle and criminal conduct was repealed in April 2021 when Governor Kay Ivey signed the removal of archaic references to homosexuality and HIV/AIDS. Sexual orientation and gender identity have been applied to sex under Title VII in Eleventh Circuit jurisdiction since 2020 and 2011 respectively, giving a federal employment route that state law does not provide.
localsOnly:
Alabama residents face the surgical-intervention requirement for changing the gender marker on a birth certificate or driver's licence, sustained by the Eleventh Circuit's September 2024 judgment and the December 2024 entry of judgment. In practice most trans residents carry identity documents that do not match their presentation.

Residents under 19 cannot lawfully receive gender-affirming care from any medical provider in the state; the offence is a Class C felony carrying 10 years, and the ban has been enforceable since August 2023 with no challenge outstanding after May 2025.

State employment, housing and public accommodations provide no gender-identity protection, and no state law bars insurance exclusions for transgender healthcare or requires trans-inclusive state employee health benefits. The protections that exist are municipal: Birmingham since September 2017 and Montevallo since April 2018 cover all four areas, while Huntsville, Tuscaloosa and Montgomery cover public employment only.

Trans residents have no standing under Alabama's hate-crime statute, which has never been amended to include gender identity; an attempt to add sexual orientation, HB533, passed the House in April 2009 by 46 to 41 but received no Senate vote before adjournment on 15 May 2009, and HB413 in 2016 and HB8 in 2017 also failed.

Public school and collegiate sport and school bathroom access are fixed to sex assigned at birth for residents as well as visitors, and Senate Bill 79 of February 2025 restates gender as an immutable binary for state purposes.
outOfScopeNotes:
The March 2024 bill that would bar university bathroom use not aligned with sex assigned at birth is described in the sources as proposed; its enactment status is unresolved in this inventory. The July 2026 assessment attributes a college-campus bathroom ban to Alabama's 'Don't Say Gay' legislation, and whether that reflects an enacted measure or the assessment's grouping is not settled here.

The 3.8 per 100,000 annual killing rate for trans women is stated by the source as an undercount floor on a 428-victim dataset spanning 2008-2025. The source does not give an Alabama victim count, an annual breakdown or a population denominator of its own, so the precision of the rate cannot be verified from this inventory.

The scope of Senate Bill 79's separate single-sex space clause — whether it reaches privately operated venues, hotels or healthcare settings used by visitors, as opposed to state-run spaces — is not addressed by the sources.

Whether the Eleventh Circuit's Title VII holdings on gender identity produce a practical federal complaint route in Alabama employment, and how they interact with the absence of state public-accommodations protection for a visitor denied service, is not sourced here.
